assessment.answer:
Control 1.6.1 (reporting of information security events and observations): the evidence shows a largely implemented reporting process, with gaps in the definition scope and in external-party reporting. This is not a compliance or certification statement.

Evidence for the implemented parts:
- Duty and channels: the security event reporting procedure (v2.0) states that "Every employee must report security events straight away," that the reporting duty is part of the employment contract, and that "The security desk is the single point of contact for all reports," reachable by email, IT service portal ticket, or the security hotline (ext. 4400) for urgent matters, with after-hours forwarding to the on-call administrator.
- Triage and priority: the procedure requires recording within one working day, sorting into personnel/physical/IT, classifying as observation, weakness or incident, and priority low/medium/high/critical, with critical reports passed to the information security officer at once.
- Ownership: personnel events go to HR, physical to the facility manager, IT to the IT operations lead, with a named deputy for each owner.
- Feedback (S6): the procedure requires feedback within two working days. The security event register summary (43 reports: 31 by email/ticket, 12 by hotline) states that every reporter received feedback within two working days; the selected entries show feedback dates for each sampled case.
- Awareness: the procedure is published on the intranet (page views from 163 of 171 employees). Training covers how to report, and briefings were sent after incidents (e.g., 158 employees confirmed reading the briefing after incident 2026-007).
- Worked examples: the register shows phishing (2026-007), a physical weakness (2026-015), a personnel observation (2026-022) and a supplier-reported breach (2026-031, critical, feedback the next day), so reports from a supplier were received and handled.

Gaps and limits:
- Definition (M1): the procedure distinguishes observation, weakness and incident and names personnel, physical and IT categories. No passage found explicitly defines reportable events for suppliers and business partners, and the register categories are only IT, physical and personnel. The physical examples (intrusion, unauthorised access, vulnerabilities in security zones) are only partly visible in the sampled entries.
- External parties (S4): no documented reporting channel for external parties other than employees was found. The supplier portal is used for change notices, and the network standard says suppliers work on site, but I found no published instruction for suppliers or customers on how to report, nor a timeliness target specific to external reports (the general two-working-day feedback and one-working-day recording rules apply).
- Training (S3): the basic course and its completion rate were not evidenced in the records. Only target-group sessions (administrators 9/9, managers 20/22, customer-network briefings 11/11) are shown. The e-learning completion records are referenced but not provided.
- Accessibility (S5): intranet publication is evidenced for employees; contractor and supplier access to the reporting procedure is not evidenced beyond the general change notices.
- Severity channels (S2): the hotline provides a real-time route for urgent events, and it is staffed during working hours with an on-call fallback. Whether this is tested is not evidenced.

Overall: the evidence supports the common point of contact (S1), feedback to reporters (S6), and a risk-based classification and channel set (M2, M3). The evidence is weaker on the supplier/business-partner scope of the definition (M1), the external-party reporting channel (S4), and proof of universal training completion (S3). These items should be checked before the control is assessed as met.

assessment.answer:
Control 1.6.2 (reported security events): the evidence shows partial management. It is not demonstrated as fully met.

What the evidence shows:
- Processing and timeliness (M1): The security event reporting procedure (v2.0) requires every report to be recorded in the security event register within one working day, and critical reports to go to the information security officer at once. The selected register entries match this: first actions were taken the same day or the next day (e.g. 2026-007 received 11 Feb, first action 11 Feb, closed 13 Feb; 2026-031 received and actioned 19 Jul, closed 24 Jul). Reporter feedback is recorded for each sampled entry.
- Reaction (M2): The sampled entries show concrete actions. Examples: 2026-007 (phishing, two users) led to password resets, session termination and sender blocking; 2026-031 (supplier breach, Critical) led to staff password resets and checks of files received; 2026-040 (unknown USB stick) led to port blocking. A briefing on 2026-007 went to all employees on 16 Feb 2026, with 158 confirming they read it.
- Categorisation and prioritisation (S1): Reports are sorted into Personnel, Physical or IT and typed as Observation, Weakness or Incident, with priority Low, Medium, High or Critical. The procedure uses "weakness" where the requirement names "security vulnerability"; "not security relevant" and "suggested improvement" are not visible as defined qualification levels in the documents reviewed.
- Lessons learned (M3): This is the main gap. The procedure requires a review after every high or critical incident, and the register states that no review meeting has been recorded yet for incidents 2026-007 (High) and 2026-031 (Critical). The policy review clause (after any serious incident) is documented, but no completed review or resulting change record was found for these incidents.
- Responsibilities and coordination (S2): The security desk is the single point of contact, and urgent reports go to a hotline that is forwarded to the on-call administrator outside working hours. Managers are trained on incident handling. However, no responsibilities matrix by category, no coordination rule for incidents that span personnel, physical and cyber categories, no qualification requirements, and no deputy or absence rules for the security desk or the information security officer were found.
- Criminal reporting (S3): No strategy for reporting potentially criminal aspects of security incidents to authorities was found in the policies searched. Incident 2026-031 (supplier breach) and 2026-007 (phishing) have no recorded decision on whether a report to authorities was considered.
- Log-review feed: Two log-review findings (2026-028 and 2026-039) were passed to the security desk, but their register entries were not in the sample, so their processing could not be verified.
- Related vulnerability handling (context only): Patch reports CVE-2026-27730 (ERP, Medium) three days overdue, moved to the 14 Nov 2026 maintenance window. A risk acceptance (RA-2026-03) exists for CVE-2026-22510 on the CAD vault server.

Overall: event intake, recording, timely first action, and documented responses are evidenced for the sampled cases. Lessons-learned follow-up for the two high/critical incidents is not evidenced, and the category responsibilities, absence management and criminal-reporting strategy (S2, S3) are not evidenced in the documents reviewed. Auditor follow-up: obtain the review records for 2026-007 and 2026-031, the criminal-reporting decision or strategy, and the responsibility and absence arrangements for the security desk.

assessment.answer:
Control 4.1.2 (user access and authentication): the documented design is largely in place, but the records do not yet show that the strongest requirements are implemented for every account type. This is not a compliance or certification statement.

Documented design (policies):
- Authentication standard: sign-in methods are chosen by risk. Internet-reachable systems (email, supplier portal, approved cloud services) require a second factor; office-only systems may use a password alone. The IT operations lead makes this choice at introduction and reviews it when exposure changes (M1 design).
- Passwords: at least 12 characters, blocked against known breach lists, no forced expiry, change immediately if exposed (S2 design, consistent with current practice, M2).
- Administrator accounts: separate admin accounts, and they "always require a hardware security key" (S3 design).
- Access control: least privilege, owner approval, removal within five working days, six-monthly review of all accounts including administrator and technical accounts (S1).

Implementation evidence (records):
- MFA rollout: all 171 employee accounts have an authenticator app registered. Cloud services sign-in uses the company account, so the same password and second factor apply.
- Access review (June–July 2026): 171 employee, 9 administrator, 14 supplier and 6 technical accounts were reviewed. Removals were made: 11 employee rights, 1 administrator right, 3 supplier accounts (left active after jobs ended), 2 technical rights. All removals were completed by 10 July 2026.
- Logging covers sign-ins, failed sign-ins and admin actions on the directory, email, ERP and CAD vault. Monthly log reviews found a suspicious account (40 failed sign-ins from abroad, escalated as 2026-028) and an unticketed CAD rights change (escalated as 2026-039).
- Training: administrators attended the privileged-accounts session (9 of 9).

Gaps and open points for the auditor:
1. No record of a per-system authentication risk assessment. The standard describes the process, but the records show exposure per system (logging scope list) rather than the chosen authentication method per system (M1 evidence incomplete).
2. Hardware security keys for the 9 administrator accounts are required by policy, but no record shows they are issued or used. The MFA record covers only employee accounts (S3 not evidenced).
3. Supplier accounts (14) and technical accounts (6) have no MFA evidence. Supplier access to the internet-facing supplier portal falls under the policy's second-factor rule, so this is a gap against the policy's own standard.
4. No record shows the breach-list password blocking or the 12-character rule is enforced in the directory (S2 design is documented; implementation is not evidenced).
5. Vulnerability context (Patch, 3 Nov 2026): CVE-2026-29871 (CVSS 7.5, directory and ERP) is scheduled for 14 Nov 2026. CVE-2026-27730 (CVSS 5.3, ERP) was 3 days overdue and has been moved to the same window. CVE-2026-22510 (CVSS 6.1, CAD vault server) is under risk acceptance RA-2026-03, which is reviewed on 15 Jan 2027. These items affect the directory and ERP that authenticate users, so they should be tracked against this control.

Overall: design is documented for risk-based authentication, password rules and admin hardware keys, and employee MFA and access reviews are evidenced. Evidence is missing for administrator hardware keys, supplier and technical account authentication, the per-system risk assessment, and password-rule enforcement. The control should be reported as partially evidenced until these gaps are closed.

assessment.answer:
Control 4.1.3 (user accounts and login information): the evidence shows a largely documented and partly operating process, with clear gaps. This is not a compliance or certification statement.

Evidence by requirement:

- M1 (create, change, delete): Supported. The account-management procedure requires a ticket, approval by the system owner, and standard-role defaults. The joiner/leaver record (Jan–Sep 2026: 12 joiners, 7 movers, 9 leavers) states every joiner was approved before creation. The sample tickets (e.g., IT-2026-0231 mover, same-day rights removal) support this.
- M2 (unique, personal accounts): Supported by policy ("Accounts are never shared between people"). Administrator rights sit in separate admin accounts. No account-level test beyond the policy was found.
- M3 (shared accounts regulated): Policy allows shared accounts only for a production-hall display terminal that cannot change data, and requires an account register entry. The account register itself was not found in the records, so the register is unverified.
- M4 (disable immediately on leaving): Partly supported for employees. Policy: disable by end of last working day. Sample leavers were disabled the same day (e.g., 2026-04-30 at 17:40; 2026-08-29 at 16:05). Gap: the access review found three supplier accounts still active after their jobs had ended. Purchasing has since committed to notify IT, but the effectiveness of that change has not been evidenced.
- M5 (regular review): Partly supported. Access-control policy requires six-monthly reviews. The June/July 2026 review covered 171 employee, 9 admin, 14 supplier, 6 technical accounts and 14 roles, with 11 + 6 + 1 + 3 + 2 removals recorded. Monthly log reviews are also recorded. Gap: accounts our staff hold in customers' systems were explicitly out of scope.
- M6 (secure delivery of login information): Policy only. Starting passwords must not be sent by email; they are handed over in person or by text to the user's own phone. No delivery records were found to confirm practice.
- M7 (login-information policy): Largely covered by the acceptable-use policy and the account-management procedure: no disclosure (including to managers or the service desk), no writing down or plain-file storage, change on suspected compromise, no reuse for private accounts, and change of initial passwords at first login. The directory settings (14 Aug 2026) show minimum length 12, breached-password checking, no expiry, and lockout after 10 failures. Events were handled in line with this (e.g., phishing incident 2026-007 with password resets; supplier breach 2026-031 with staff password resets). The authentication standard 3.1 was not retrieved, so the full quality requirements could not be checked against it.
- S1 (basic account): Supported. New accounts get only the standard employee role.
- S2 / S7 (default vendor accounts and passwords disabled or blocked): No evidence found.
- S3 (created or authorised by responsible body): Supported via system-owner approval.
- S4 (four-eyes approval): Supported by the sampled joiner and mover tickets.
- S5 (service-provider accounts disabled on task completion): Not met in practice. Three supplier accounts stayed active after their jobs ended. Remediation was announced but not yet verified.
- S6 (deadlines for disabling and deleting): Supported. Disable by end of last working day; delete after 90 days (sample IT-2026-0588 deleted 90 days after disabling).
- S8 (secure use of authentication medium): Partly evidenced. All 171 employee accounts have an authenticator app registered. How the device/second factor is protected was not evidenced.
- S9 (regular review including customer systems): Partly met. Internal reviews are regular, but customer-system accounts are excluded from the review scope.
- S10 (no interactive login for technical accounts): No evidence found. Six technical accounts were reviewed, with two rights removed, but logon restriction was not verified.

Overall: strong documented controls for account creation, approval, leaver disablement and periodic review, and a credible password and MFA setup. Open gaps before this control could be considered fully met: supplier-account offboarding (S5), review of accounts in customer systems (S9), evidence for default-account blocking (S2/S7), technical-account interactive-logon prevention (S10), evidence of secure delivery of initial credentials (M6), and the shared-account register (M3).

assessment.answer:
Control 4.2.1 (access rights assignment and management): the company's own evidence shows that most of the control is documented and operating, with open points on M2 (customer systems), on revocation after role changes, and on one rights change made without a ticket. This does not establish compliance.

M1 (must): Partly evidenced.
- Application and approval: The access control policy ("Asking for access") and the account management procedure ("New accounts") require a ticket and owner approval before IT grants rights. The joiner/leaver sample (January to September 2026: 12 joiners, 7 movers, 9 leavers) shows approvals by the ERP or CAD owner. The summary states that every joiner account was approved by the system owner before creation.
- Least privilege: The policy says rights not needed for the job are refused, and new accounts start with a standard employee role only.
- Revocation: The policy requires unneeded rights to be removed within five working days. The sample shows leaver accounts disabled on the last working day (2026-04-30 and 2026-08-29) and a mover's old role removed the same day. However, the access review of 2026-06-20 removed 11 employee rights that "were left over from earlier role changes", and 3 supplier accounts for finished jobs had not been disabled when the jobs ended. Revocation after role change and at the end of supplier engagement therefore did not reliably happen before the review.
- Unticketed change: The August 2026 log review records a "rights change on the CAD vault without a ticket" (security desk reference 2026-039). The records provided do not show how this was resolved. It bypasses the approval procedure and needs to be closed out before the control can be assessed as operating.

M2 (must): Partly evidenced.
- The access control policy requires all accounts, including administrator and technical accounts, to be reviewed every six months by role owners, and the account management procedure requires a recorded six-monthly manager review. The records show a review in June/July 2026 covering 171 employee, 9 administrator, 14 supplier and 6 technical accounts, with removals recorded. The previous review was in January 2026, consistent with a six-month cycle.
- However, the review scope explicitly excludes "accounts that our staff hold in customers' systems". M2 extends the review to customers' IT systems, so this part is not evidenced.

S1 (should): Not evidenced as a separate documented authorisation strategy. The access control policy covers the approval process, but no separate strategy document was found.

S2 (should): Supported. Authorisation roles are in use (standard employee role; 14 roles reviewed on 2026-06-27, with 6 rights removed).

S3 (should): Largely supported. The policy requires need-based, role-based allocation, and the joiner and mover sample reflects role-based grants. The unticketed CAD vault change and the leftover rights weaken this.

S4 (should): Supported by policy ("Ordinary accounts never hold administrator rights"; administrator rights only on separate admin accounts). The administrator review covered 9 admin accounts and removed one unneeded server group right. The records do not directly test whether any ordinary account held admin rights.

S5 (should): Partly evidenced. The mover sample shows rights updated the same day, but the 11 leftover employee rights from earlier role changes show that updates after responsibility changes were not always made.

Related, outside this control: the June 2026 log review flagged one account with 40 failed sign-ins from abroad (reference 2026-028). The records do not show its outcome.

Open points for the auditor: (1) extend the access review to accounts in customers' systems (M2); (2) evidence the handling and closure of the unticketed CAD vault rights change (2026-039) and the outcome of 2026-028; (3) show that role-change and supplier-end revocations happen on time, without relying on the periodic review to catch them; (4) provide a separate authorisation strategy if S1 is to be evidenced.

What the evidence supports:

The network and transfer register (checked 8 Sep 2026) lists TLS 1.2 or newer for company email and the supplier portal, and TLS 1.3 plus encryption at rest for the customer exchange platform. An external TLS scan on 8 Sep 2026 found no service accepting unencrypted connections and none offering a protocol older than TLS 1.2. This is relevant to M1 for data in transit.
- The cloud services register records that confidential mail passes the mail filter only end-to-end encrypted, and that the provider's audit report or certificate was checked for the listed services.
- The information security policy 4.0 (approved 14 Jul 2026) and the encryption standard 1.2 are published on the intranet, and the encryption standard is listed as a supporting standard with an owner.

- The encryption standard passages retrieved for "Approved methods" (AES-128+, RSA-3072+ or ECC-256+, SHA-256+), "Keys" (creation, recovery keys, withdrawal, renewal) and "Monthly check" (laptop encryption) are flagged as stale in the index. Control 5.2.5 (vulnerabilities identified and addressed): the evidence supports parts of the control. It does not support a full assessment, and nothing here amounts to a compliance or certification finding.

Evidence reviewed: Patch vulnerability status answered 3 November 2026; information security policy (approved 14 July 2026); network and transfer standard; network services register (TLS test, 8 September 2026). I found no patch management standard, no patch-testing record, and no record verifying that installed patches took effect.

M1 (gather and evaluate vulnerability information): Supported. Patch collects manufacturer advisories and CVE entries every night and scores them with CVSS 3.1. The tracked list shows CVSS scores for five CVEs (3.1 to 9.8).

M2 (identify affected systems and assess risk): Largely supported. Each tracked CVE is mapped to affected assets (email gateway, directory, ERP, CAD vault server, office printers) and given a priority (Critical, High, Medium, Low). The review covers the systems in the asset list only. The policy document does not describe the risk-assessment method.

M3 (treat risks): Partly supported.
- CVE-2026-31244 (CVSS 9.8, email gateway): ticket PT-118 closed 21 October 2026, before its 24 October due date.
- CVE-2026-18402 (CVSS 3.1, printers): ticket PT-121 closed 28 October 2026.
- CVE-2026-29871 (CVSS 7.5, directory and ERP): update scheduled for 14 November 2026, which is before its due date. Still open at the status date.
- CVE-2026-27730 (CVSS 5.3, ERP): due 31 October 2026 and 3 days overdue. It was moved to the 14 November 2026 maintenance window by the IT operations lead. This is an informal reschedule, not a documented risk acceptance, and it should be formally recorded or escalated.
- CVE-2026-22510 (CVSS 6.1, CAD vault server): risk accepted under RA-2026-03 (managing director, 30 September 2026). The vendor has no fix for the installed version and the server is replaced in March 2027. Review is set for 15 January 2027.

S1 (adequate patch management defined and implemented): Not evidenced. The information security policy's list of supporting standards does not include a patch management standard, and no patch-testing or deployment procedure was found. Patch tickets are tracked, but I could not confirm the process.

S2 (risk-minimising measures): Partly supported. For the CAD vault server under RA-2026-03, interim measures are documented: it is reachable only from the design VLAN and downloads are logged. Note that the August 2026 log review recorded a rights change on the CAD vault without a ticket (passed to the security desk as 2026-039). Its outcome is not shown in the evidence.

S3 (verification of successful patch installation): Not evidenced. Closed tickets (PT-118, PT-121) show that work was closed, but there is no record confirming the installed version or patch state afterwards.

Overall: vulnerability information is gathered and scored, and affected assets and priorities are identified. Treatment is in progress: two critical or low items are closed, one high and one medium item are scheduled, one medium item is overdue and rescheduled, and one is under documented risk acceptance with interim measures. The patch management standard and post-installation verification are not evidenced. Open items for the auditor: obtain the patch management procedure, evidence of patch testing and post-patch verification for PT-118 and PT-121, the formal decision for CVE-2026-27730, and the outcome of security desk case 2026-039.
